claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is single-phase, nearly equimolar, homogenized, solutionized, and contains minimal secondary phases.
Short-range chemical ordering in equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi modifies dislocation slip pathways.
Short-range chemical ordering in CoCrFeNiTi modifies stacking-fault energies.
Short-range chemical ordering produces moderate hardness and strength together with enhanced plasticity and machinability in CoCrFeNiTi relative to other Ti-bearing HEAs.
Changing aging or solutionization time and temperature can vary the degree of short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi.
Short-range order manifests as sub-nanometer compositional fluctuations in CoCrFeNiTi.
These sub-nanometer compositional fluctuations locally pin or assist dislocation motion.
Increasing short-range order raises slip-energy barriers and thereby increases hardness and strength.
Lower short-range order eases dislocation glide and maintains good plasticity.
Relative to minimally ordered solutionized CoCrFeNiTi, more strongly ordered material will have higher yield strength and hardness.
Relative to minimally ordered solutionized CoCrFeNiTi, more strongly ordered material will have lower uniform elongation from 25 to 600 °C.
In HEAs, lattice deformation can impede dislocation migration and increase strength and hardness.
Composition, lattice distortion, grain distribution, defects, and phase constitution can influence HEA yield strength and post-yield behavior.
The proposed tests cover tension or compression between room temperature and 600 °C at strain rates of 10^-3 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi made by standard vacuum melting and solutionization and tested at temperatures no higher than 600 °C.
Atom-probe tomography or diffuse scattering can be used to establish a difference in short-range order between comparison groups.
Statistically identical mechanical responses despite a proven difference in short-range order would falsify the proposed SRO-controlled mechanical response.
Distinct mechanical responses in the absence of detectable short-range order would falsify the hypothesis.
